#1311. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

Jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the new arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

Sidiki Cherif with a STUNNING finish on his first Premier League start! 🤩 https://t.co/EoTB8VCHuR

It should have been three. Again Wissa was partly to blame, losing the ball in midfield to set Coventry on the counter-attack. When Botman made a mess of a clearance it spun perfectly into the path of Cherif. The net should have bulged but the £20m summer signing from Fenerbahce scuffed wide.

The visitors needed something special to get back into it and it came from the most unlikely of sources as Botman unleashed a rocket from 25 yards.

Sven Botman, that is SENSATIONAL! 🤯 https://t.co/GalkqMs5ZE

In a flash the balance of play shifted in Newcastle’s favour. They poured forward in search of the equaliser. Jaissle switched to a 4-4-2 with Will Osula joining Fernandez-Pardo up front, but instead of pulling level, Coventry pulled further ahead.

"We need to improve the things we can control, and right now that's a lot" 🗣️ Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle expresses his disappointment after his side's loss to Coventry 👇 https://t.co/fatJkZYyRM

Very, very satisfying. It’s so hard to win. We played like the team we want to be here. A team you look at and go there’s so much energy and spirit in the group. We know we are going to have to suffer this season, when we don’t have a lot of the ball. We have to understand it. The level is what it is.

The work ethic, the belief. You get what you deserve. Great finishes. We haven’t quite had the rub of the green this season and that might have helped us nick a couple of more points. I’m a firm believer that you keep going. It was a complete performance. We’ve got to keep our feet on the ground because we’re going to have to do 30+ of those but it’s a great feeling for the players.

[Cherif] is very, very exciting because he is so young. He has got a really good manner. He wants to train, he wants to learn. He’s quite quiet but on the pitch he shows a lot of personality. When you see the quality of the strike and the hold-up play, there’s a lot to come from him.

"That one was for you, nan" Jack Rudoni explains his goal celebration ❤️ https://t.co/79OvHMlu6J

A victory to savour for Coventry whose teenagers Cherif and Mfuni scored fine goals. No doubt they wobbled when Botman equalised and for the next 10 minutes but Newcastle blew too many chances and resumed making errors at the back. Newcastle’s squad is a mess.

Newcastle might maintain that Thomas-Asante was offside and blocking the keeper’s view when Mfuni pulled the trigger but I think Hornicke had a clear view and hence it wasn’t an offence.

The first two minutes of stoppage time, of which there are four, pass without incident.

Osula lifts a volley over the bar with a wild attempt. Toure was injured in the build-up and will be replaced by Dan Burn.

Never mind Bob Gelodof and Brenda Ann Spencer, Matthias Jaissle doesn’t like Mondays. They are 8-2 down on Monday Night Football so far this season.

Coventry 4 Newcastle 1 (Mfuni) The substitute had only just replaced Rudoni and took the ball on the inside-left 25 yards out, advanced then wrapped his instep around a left-foot shot, arrowing it across Hornicek into the bottom right.

Stephen Mfuni makes his mark for Coventry! 👊 https://t.co/KI2kgpfUJP

Thomas-Asante crashes a right-foot shot into the heart of the left post. A thumping strike that leaves the metalwork ringing.

Coventry 3 Newcastle 1 (Simms) Right foot shot from 18 yards through Thiaw’s legs, clipping the inside of his right knee to deflect it into the bottom left. Joelinton had been trying to dribble it out of the box, overhit it and fouled Thomas-Asante as he tried to recover. The whistle was betweeen the ref’s lips but he did not exhale as Simms steered his shot through Thiaw’s legs.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

Touré beats Dasilva for pace down the right then blazes over from a tight angle then moments later is given an opportunity to shoot and sticks it in the stands again. Both times the cross was on.

Toure has caused untold problems for Dasilva. Newcastle corner on the left is bent far too deep and goes out for a goal-kick.

Wissa dithers over a shot when found by Toure to the right of the penalty spot and finally clips it into Thomas. Coventry are clinging on but flapping. As is the crowd.

Hall, following Botman’s lead, lets fly from distance, straight at Rushworth.

Coventry fluff a couple of chances to break with hasty, panicked passes.

It was as if Coventry were defying him to have a shot. And in doing so, the nerves are back with a bang in the crowd.

Coventry 2 Newcastle 1 (Botman) Coventry invite him to shoot by backing off and backing off and he RSVPs with a left-foot torpedo from 20 yards into the roof of the net. What a strike!

Sven Botman, that is SENSATIONAL! 🤯 https://t.co/GalkqMs5ZE

Barnes appears to have been brought down by Sakamoto in the Coventry penalty area but he was offside. One of Jaissle’s staff is booked for some verbal transgression.

Joelinto rattles bones in a tackle that was not shown as they focus on Barnes’ spurious penalty appeal when he slipped behind Pinnock.

Rudoni dips his shoulder and skins Botman in the Newcastle box but tries and fails to square it to Cherif instead of shooting.

Touré makes ground down the right and slips Joelinton down the inside. The substitute, who took the captain’s armband off Thiaw, tries to find Pardo with a cross that Thomas blocks.

Now Willock blazes over from eight yards on the right after a slick one-two with Murphy.

Dedic → MileyTouré → MurphyJoelinton → Willock

Rushworth drops Hall’s cross but recovers to grab it on the bounce. Jaissle has three subs stripped. Murphy tries to bend a cross from the right to Barnes at the back post but Van Ewijk and Thomas combine to scramble it out for a throw-in.

Now Cherif misses a gilded opportunity after a hacked clearance from Botman lands at his feet to the left of the spot. He kicks it into his other leg and the ball dribbles wide. The way Botman dealt with Thomas-Asante’s cross was really shoddy.

Barnes disguises his inside run and evades Van Ewijk to collect Thiaw’s pass up the inside-right channel. He spins and feeds it infield to Wissa who telegraphs his shot with a laboured touch before swiinging a right-footer from 25 yards straight down Rushworth’s throat.

Newcastle have been awful. Seem to lack leadership and heft on the field. The return of Joelinton can’t come quick enough.

Coventry 2 Newcastle 0 (Cherif) Talented lad. Absolutely larrups a right-foot shot through a thicket of Newcastle legs from 18 yards when a long throw was headed out to the edge of the box.

Sidiki Cherif with a STUNNING finish on his first Premier League start! 🤩 https://t.co/EoTB8VCHuR

Collison between Van Ewijk and Willock leaves them both winded and needing treatment. The Newcastle midfielder had been trying to bullock down the middle in purusit of a pass.

Coventry overload with seven men on the right before rolling the kick-off to the left-footed Rushworth who launches it too far up that wing and Hornicek gathers.

Interesting half for Matias Fernandez-Pardo who has been in the middle of most of Newcastle’s best moments but has failed to take two excellent chances.

The first was baffling as the Belgium international made no attempt to sweep in Jacob Murphy’s cutback at the near post, letting it run through his legs thinking Harvey Barnes was in a better position. He wasn’t.

The second was a little unfortunate as he did well to time his run and wriggle free of centre back Bobby Thomas. That put him in on goal with just the goalkeeper to beat, but having sat Chris Rushworth down he pushed the ball a fraction too wide and by the time he was in a position to shoot, Thomas had done brilliantly to cut off the angle and block it.

Coventry have been good but Newcastle have been really poor again away from home. They are yet to put a 90-minute performance together since the opening weekend against Liverpool. Matthias Jaissle will want a lot more from his team in the second half.

Newcastle should at least be level given their chances but you have to admire Coventry’s spirit and work rate. Cherif seems to me to have a high ceiling and at 19 is already a real handful.

Newcastle need to stop fannying around and buy a proper centre-forward. Wissa is better wide or in a more fluid system, as I suspect Fernandez-Pardo is, too. Stick Osula on and get the chequebook out in January. Offer Boro £50m for Lankshear.

Cheeif, working his socks off, chases a lost cause and retrieves a long pass forward in the whitewash but when he turns to try to play it to Thomas-Asante, Thiaw makes a good tackle.

Hall turns away Mason-Clark’s effort from the left and the game turns into a basketball match… without the scoring as both sides fly from end to end.  Two minutes of stoppage time to come.

Thomas to the rescue again, He was outpaced by Fernandez-Pardo running on to straight ball down the middle but kept on going when the Belgium forward rounded the keeper to block the shot. Fernandez-Pardo may have been better off taking on the shot earlier, surprising the advancing Rushworth, rather than trying to take him out of the equation. Or dinked it before he got too close.

Bobby Thomas does brilliantly to deny Fernandez-Pardo 👏 https://t.co/dB4Qk0uoCu

Willock is penalised for grabbing Yirenkyi to concede a free-kick hjust inside the Newcastle half. Rudoni tries to float it into the box but overclubs it and it sails behind for a goal-kick.

Willock tries to replicate Doku’s goal from yesterday, swinging a right-foot shot from the left into the top right but Yirenkyi stood firm and deflected it wide. Coventry defend the corner solidly and tear off upfield but the diligent Barnes races back 70 yards to mop up.

Newcastle force Coventry all the way back to Rushworth who knocks it long to Dasilva who holds it up well and passes to Mason-Clark. The left-winger runs and then tries to force the ball through Thiaw instead of laying it back to the left-back who was free. Thiaw makes the block.

Hornicek, rushed into a clearance, makes haste to belt it away from danger.

Thomas, who made a goal-line clearance at Forest, heads the ball away from an open goal a couple of yards out after Murphy’s effort bobbled up off Rushworth. Excellent cross from Barnes to the back post.

End to end after Fernandez-Pardo at the near post is in the right position to hook in a shot from Murphy’s cross but he dummies instead and there was no one behind him. Was he put off by a defender’s shout? Coventry break and storm down the inside-right, Cherif closing in on goal and refusing the entreaties of Mason-Clark and Rudoni to pass inside. he shoots straight at Hornicek.

Newcastle think they should have a corner and they are right after Van Ewijk’s block of Fernandez-Pardo’s cross took a double deflection back off the Coventry right-back. To set up that raid down the wing, Willock bullied Yirenkyi off the ball on halfway.

Coventry break the siege with a clearance that allows Mason-Clark to shield the ball and buy a throw-in on the left. The ref warns Van Ewijk not to take too long over it after taking his time to jog over from the other wing.

Coventry are playing a dangerous game now and Newcastle have all the momentum, stringing passes together and using their wide players well.

Barnes sticks out his right foot in the Coventry box and steers a shot wide from Willock’s cross/shot. Thomas had earlier intercepted Murphy’s dipping cross to nod it away from Fernandez-Pardo as Coventry retreat.

Barnes passes blind back to Hornicek unaware that Cherif was lurking. But the Czech goalkeeper is more alert and darts out to clear.

Botman, who has never looked the same since his injury, heads the ball out for a throw-in. Van Ewijk hurls it into the box but Newcastle deal with it well and break in numbers with Fernandez-Pardo carrying the ball the last 30 yards. But he submits to summit fever when he approaches the box. Barnes is in space to his left but he chops to his right, looking for an opportunity to shoot but can’t find one then forces a pass beyond Murphy who had left his wing. Coventry pick it off but butcher the counter-attack with a rubbish pass to Cherif that was off target.

Thomas, the right-sided centre-back, strides out of defence and sees Cherif loitering on Botman’s shoulder but overhits his pass down the inside-right channel.

Hall sends Fernandez-Pardo down the left and the forward retrieves it just by the byline. He cuts it back to Willock who spins to tee up Barnes to fire a left-foot daisy-cutter from 18 yards straight at Rushworth.

Terrible goalkeeping from Lukasz Hornicek who made one mistake and followed it up with another diving at full stretch at the feet of a Coventry player in the box. He did not need to go after the ball as there was no imminent danger.

Sidiki Cherif knew he only needed to get a touch on it before the Newcastle goalkeeper. Such a soft penalty to give away early on away from home.

Newcastle have not started the game well but the goalkeeper will have a lot of explaining to do after that one

“First home Premier League goal for 25 years” – yes but it’s only their third Premier League game for 25 years.

A flag catches Barnes offside. Slow start from the visitors.

Hornicke made a dog’s dinner of that. A headlong dive to try to recover his clumsy handling and Cherif beat him to it. Hotnicek swiped across his ankles and it was a stuck on penalty.

Coventry 1 Newcastle 0 (Rudoni, pen) Takes it with his left foot. Hornicek thinks he’s going into the bottom right but he cocks his ankle to sweep it into the bottom left.

Jack Rudoni converts to give to Coventry their first goal at home since returning to the Premier League! 🙌 https://t.co/Q7la7nYwoq

Mistake by Hornicek and then he appears to bring down Cherif diving to retrieve it.

Yes, definitely a pen even though VAR took its time.

Good atmosphere. The home fans are making a racket.

Noticeable that Yirenkyi slots in being Van Ewijk when the full-back goes forward. Miley, who is playing at right-back, intercepts a chip up to Mason-Clark and works the ball back to Hornicek.

As the strains of We’ll Live and Die in These Towns dies down to segue into the Eton Boating Song, Newcastle kick off, attacking from right to left. When they lose the ball Wissa is penalised for tripping Rudoni 45 yards out.

Coventry are in blue and white stripes, harking back to the 1987 Cup final rather than the Mick Coop years. Newcastle are in vibrant lilac.

It was good to get a win. We worked very hard for it. It’s so hard to get wins, especially on the road. And now we’re back at home and we have to work on those attributes [that earned us the win] at Forest. We rotated pretty well, there are different aspects of the game we want to improve on regardless of shape.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

The 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

#1310. Why Everton School Visits Are Making A Mark

“Captain Underpants”. The laughter that follows is infectious. It seems doubtful that it was an honest answer to the question posed to Zach Lee by the young boy located somewhere near the front of the classroom: “What is your favourite book?” But it got exactly the reaction he was after.

The room is abuzz. It has been for much of the past hour.

Goalkeeper Lee and five of his Everton Under-21s teammates have gleefully taken up the task of being reading buddies to the children of Ellesmere Port’s Meadow Primary School, one of six schools that make up the recently renamed Everton Multi-Academy Trust (EMAT). Seven miles away, six of their Under-21 peers are doing likewise at Oldfield Primary School in Chester.

Nearer to Liverpool, the hollers that greeted Everton Women’s Holly McNamara and Karen Holmgaard 24 hours earlier are still reverberating around the corridors of Bidston Avenue Primary School.

Christian Nørgaard and close friends Tyler Dibling and Tyrique George are also familiar with the noise the pupils at the Birkenhead school can make. Last month, the trio were serenaded with a ukulele rendition of Spirit of the Blues on a visit there. Blue ukuleles, of course.

If the colour of the musical instruments is a cute indicator of the strengthening ties between the football club and the EMAT schools, the time being spared by the players is of much greater significance.

It is intended to demonstrate a cross-Club connection with EMAT, which sits alongside Everton in the Community as one of Everton’s associated organisations. “Part of the Everton family,” as Everton’s Chief Tax and Sustainability Officer and Chair of Trustees for EMAT Alison Haynes puts it.

But there is a deeper intention, too. “We want to use the power of the Everton crest to inspire and engage youngsters in education,” says Steven Baker OBE, CEO of EMAT. Baker has seen this in evidence for more than a decade, having previously served as Principal of Everton Alternative Provision Free School, the award-winning L4 facility that offers youngsters who have struggled in mainstream schools a route back into education.

Lee and his Under-21 colleagues, McNamara and Holmgaard are all supporting one particular mission of EMAT - to inspire youngsters towards a life-long love of reading. More immediately, to ensure they have the requisite literacy level to adequately prepare them for what lies ahead in secondary school education.

In Ellesmere Port, Chester and Birkenhead, the players are tackling their role head on. Books - donated by Everton staff to help replenish the schools’ libraries - are strewn across the tables and spilling onto the floor. No-one’s troubled by the mess.

Julia Donaldson’s greatest hits are being played out across the room. Michael Morpurgo – a childhood favourite author of midfielder Jack Patterson – can be heard, too. ‘Bluey’ is an appropriately named hit on another table. And then there’s Lee and a group of little ones giggling at Captain Underpants.

Close by to the classroom at Meadow, Everton’s leading post-war goalscorer Graeme Sharp is here too, continuing the literacy theme by officially opening the school’s newly-refurbished library.

“These children will remember today,” says Baker. “They will remember players from Everton coming into school and taking the time to sit with them.

“They love hearing stories but they also love having someone to read to. Both aspects are so important for a child’s development.”

As is music. It’s why Dibling, George and Norgaard found themselves being taught the chords to one of Goodison’s – and now Hill Dickinson Stadium’s – favourite tunes last month.

Studies show a direct correlation between a child mastering a musical instrument and making their mark in maths and other creative fields.

The Toffees trio left behind gifts of recorders (blue ones), helping the school expand the opportunities it can offer to its pupils.

“We find it’s really important for their resilience and it's good for the children mentally and socially to have the opportunity to not only play an instrument, but to play to an audience,” says Bidston Avenue headteacher Stuart Brady, a Tranmere Rovers fan.

“It's great for us as a school to have the connection we do with Everton and the players. Days like this are great, but it's also about the children feeling they belong to something bigger.”

And the proof that EMAT is getting it right is stacking up. In 2024, Everton Free School and Everton Football College – the two original schools on which the Trust was founded – were jointly awarded an ‘Outstanding’ rating by Ofsted. Earlier this year, the respected national TES Awards named EMAT (then The People’s Learning Trust) as its Trust of the Year for trusts with nine schools or fewer.

With the support of a Premier League football club and its players behind them, it is hoped the collective will continue to go from strength to strength.

The intention is that Everton’s Under-21s will return to the schools to resume their reading buddy duties at junctures throughout the season, strengthening their bonds with the schools and pupils. It is seen as a vital part of the players’ professional development.

Representatives from the Men’s and Women’s team will continue to play their part also. Merlin Röhl has already been a guest of Oldfield Primary School’s after-school chess club, taking up an invitation to share his love of the ancient game with the next generation.

“We understand the responsibility and influence we have as a football club when it comes to our communities,” says Haynes. “And you cannot understate the impact the player visits have.

“The atmosphere and the smiles you see in the room, the energy they give to the children… it’s truly wonderful.”

#1309. Quantum physics can prove where you are

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Davide Bacco is in the Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Florence, Florence 50019, Italy.

Where you are can matter as much as who you are. Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake. Spoofing and jamming attacks on satellite navigation, for example, are on the rise. Writing in Nature, Kavuri et al.1 report an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using the peculiar correlations between quantum particles, known as entanglement. Remarkably, the scheme’s security does not rely on trust of any quantum hardware, only on measurement statistics and the fact that nothing travels faster than light.

#1308. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

A fine team move ended with an excellent Stanway finish. It was her fifth goal in this qualifying campaign and she is England’s top scorer for 2025-26.

A really good example was the away game against Ukraine in qualifying. We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half - the keeper was making saves, we hit the woodwork - but the messaging at half-time was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities.

”Not to start snatching or taking shots from distance, just trusting in our style of play and our ability to find gaps. We came out for the second half and scored really quickly. It’s just about sticking to the plan and being patient.”

Erica Meg Parkinson, one of England’s new midfielders, was apparently named after Eric Cantona.

While Cantona still famously is proud of his kung fu kick, when he attacked an obnoxious Crystal Palace fan, Parkison is less enthused by football’s most famous case of breaking the fourth wall.

“My dad is a huge Man United fan so I was named after Eric Cantona,” Parkinson says. “It’s a pretty good player to be named after except for, you know, the karate kicks.

“My brother was named after Denis Law. I don’t think my mum had much of a say in the name so she was dragged into it, but it kind of worked out because we both play football now.”

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

“That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

#1306. KILMARNOCK 2 ABERDEEN 4: Dazzling Dons get a Frick pick-up but it's more misery for McCann's men

Published: 15:33 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 16:15 EST, 21 November 2026

Having been bored senseless by the football offered up under Stephen Robinson, Aberdeen supporters were – at the very least – crying out for the next appointment to provide some sort of entertainment to get excited about over the dark winter months.

In Mario Frick, they may have got their man. Whether or not the former Luzern boss will be a success at Pittodrie is anyone’s guess. But on this evidence, it’s going to be a lot of fun watching him have a go.

At times, they were scintillating here on their way to a thrilling win which moved them five clear of their hosts and provided some much-needed breathing room ahead of a tricky upcoming schedule which involves trips to Ibrox and Tynecastle, as well as two home clashes against the Dundee clubs.

Yes, it wasn’t perfect. Far from it, in fact. Defensively, they were far too open. Kilmarnock just weren’t good enough to take full advantage.

But you suspect that will be forgiven to an extent as long as they can play with this level of panache and aggression going forward.

Findlay Marshall celebrates after scoring the Dons' fourth goal at Rugby Park

Frick has arrived with the promise of bringing ‘heavy metal’ football to Pittodrie. It’s taken a little over 90 minutes to understand what he's talking about.

‘It was very chaotic,’ he admitted. ‘It's quite different to Switzerland, because there is technicality, but it’s not as physical as it was today.

‘It was difficult. We were lucky as well because Killie, especially in the second half, played very well, but I think at the end it's a deserved victory.

‘When the players were young, they didn’t think about mistakes, didn’t think about any negatives.

‘They played only to win for fun, and I told them to play as if they were young players and I think, especially first half, it was very good.

‘You don't know what's going on or what can happen in this first game, so I'm very happy we won.’

Frick shows his delight after tasting victory in his first match in charge of Aberdeen

Kilmarnock spurned a golden opportunity to take a sixth-minute lead at the end of a rapid counter-attack, with Joe Hugill finding himself all alone in the Dons box.

The striker took a heavy first touch, allowing Marius Muller to quickly narrow the angle and block the effort. It’s easy to see why Hugill has found the back of the net just twice this year.

And the hosts were made to pay for that miss within 90 seconds as Aberdeen went in front.

For the umpteenth time this season, Killie failed to clear their lines under little pressure, with Stuart Armstrong teeing up Kevin Nisbet to sweep home a lovely finish from the edge of the area. The unsighted Nico Mantl in the Killie goal didn’t even move.

Mind you, he should have done significantly better four minutes later as Nisbet notched his second of the afternoon.

The keeper’s positioning as the Dons striker stepped up to send a low free-kick in off the post was as poor as it gets.

You got the feeling that the walls would have caved in had Aberdeen grabbed a third, but a brief drop-off in intensity from Frick’s side enabled Killie to drag themselves back into the contest.

A bit of pinball outside the Dons box saw the ball fall favourably for skipper Greg Kiltie 12 yards out, who adjusted his body brilliantly to drill beyond Muller on the half-volley.

Yet with a defence as dodgy as this, manager Neil McCann can never feel overly confident.

Ante Palaversa – terrific on his first appearance of the season – was given far too much time in the centre circle to get his head up and pick out Nesta Guinness-Walker on the left.

He glided past MJ Kamson-Kamara as if he wasn’t there before dinking a ball right on to the head of Brad Lyons, who rose completely unopposed to power home against his former employers.

If Killie continue to defend like this, relegation is a certainty. Will the manager even get the chance to turn it around? Going off the abuse being hurled in his direction from the home punters, his jacket is evidently on a shoogly peg. Many fans have already made up their mind.

Nisbet's free-kick finds the net for his second as the Dons take control of the game

Michael Schjonning-Larsen’s deflected effort from 20 yards shortly after the restart looked destined for the goal before Muller instinctively leapt to his right to claw it away on the line. It was a superb stop.

Goodness knows what the keeper was thinking as he tried to pass out from the six-yard line, playing it straight to the feet of Tyreece John-Jules – only just on the park – who steadied himself before finishing.

You would have stuck your house on Nisbet putting this one to bed with five minutes remaining, however with just Mantl to beat, he pulled his left-footed effort wide.

Findlay Marshall showed him how it’s done with stoppage-time looming, running half the length of the field before drilling low into the corner to consign Killie to another sobering defeat.

McCann said: ‘I probably sound like a broken record, but we create really big, big chances, and we don't take them.

‘We're letting games pass us by. We're giving teams the opportunity to start ahead of us because of the goals we're conceding and then it's difficult to work back.’

#1305. Dundee rout is best display of my Hearts reign so far, beams Vrancken

Published: 17:25 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 17:35 EST, 21 November 2026

Wouter Vrancken said Hearts’ ruthless 8-0 demolition of 10-man Dundee was his team’s best performance since he took charge at Tynecastle.

Sabah Kerjota and Pierre Landry Kabore both scored twice with Claudio Braga, Sabri Guendouz, Stuart Findlay and a Ryan Finnigan own goal taking the tally to eight without reply.

And Vrancken was naturally delighted that his players had ended a run of three defeats in a row in such spectacular style.

The 47-year-old said: 'The best performance? Of course.

'When you have the confidence of one moment and then you feel the score is getting bigger, you see the players with extra confidence.

'You see the dynamics there and it’s good they feel it works.

Stuart Findlay heads in the eighth to cap a remarkable evening for Hearts at Dens Park

'When it’s 0-0 and 1-0, you don’t feel as confident so maybe you don’t have the bravery to do it or show it.

'Today they did it and hopefully they felt it can work and they can show it more.

'It was ruthless and I like to see it this way. That was the message at half-time – that and keeping the clean sheet.

'I was very happy with the performance, not only the score.

'We had the talks before our days off, they were really honest and open. It was good to hear but you have to take ownership of it on the pitch.

'You can talk as much as you want but if you can’t show it on the pitch it doesn’t mean anything.

'When you do it like this it’s the first step.

'But it’s only the first step, only one game and we have to try to bring more.

“The message to the players is feet back on the ground because after the last break we started with a 5-0 win over St Mirren then had difficult moments.

'It was ruthless in the game today but the schedule is also ruthless – but we got a good boost from tonight.'

Claudio Braga fires home a fifth goal for Vrancken's side in the demolition job

Dundee boss Steven Pressley admitted he was embarrassed by the result and performance.

He said: 'It’s a night I need to own, a night where I can only apologise for the performance. I never expected that.

'I had a little sense we haven’t been quite on it over the last couple of weeks but I take ownership and I mean that.

'We talk about the culture and environment that we set and part of that is making sure we have a fully motivated team, a team which works hard and shows grit.

'We didn’t show that tonight but that is on me and I mean that.

'We looked unmotivated and lacking edge tonight.

'Tactically astute, we were miles away and that’s my responsibility.

'All areas of our performance was disappointing.

Lille are considering legal ⁠action after defender Tiago Santos suffered a serious knee injury following an “uncontrolled and dangerous” tackle in Saturday’s match ‌against Le Havre.

Santos, 24, suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal tear in his right knee and was carried off the pitch on a stretcher after being tackled by Le Havre midfielder Amir Richardson during the first half of Lille’s 1-0 victory.

The referee gave a foul for the tackle but did not issue Richardson with a caution.

Lille said the ‌tackle merited ‌a red card ⁠and that they had asked the league’s governing body (LFP) to refer the matter to its disciplinary committee. The club are also seeking an explanation of ⁠the video review process undertaken by match officials.

“LOSC is exploring all possible legal avenues and reserves the right to take any legal action necessary to obtain compensation for its losses,” the ​club said. “It will support Tiago in ‌any steps he decides to take to defend his rights.”

Will Olivier Giroud receive a warm welcome back to the Emirates Stadium? The Frenchman spent six years as an Arsenal player but burned a few bridges when he left the club for Chelsea, and then celebrated wildly when Chelsea beat Arsenal in the Europa League final of 2019. Now 40, Giroud has shown remarkable longevity and is unquestionably one of the best strikers of his generation. But can he hurt this formidable Arsenal defence? It’s a tough ask.

Olivier Giroud back at the Emirates ❤️ https://t.co/TPBgcNDsVW

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel)

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

#1302. MOTHERWELL 1 RANGERS 2: Naderi rides to the rescue as wasteful Ibrox men get out of jail with late winner

Published: 18:01 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 18:10 EST, 21 November 2026

FOR a team that just couldn’t find a way to get the ball into the net, no matter how they tried, it was always going to take a couple of jammy deflections or something out of the ordinary to get out of jail.

And that’s exactly how it panned out with just two minutes left on the clock. Rangers, tied at 1-1 and in danger of falling six points behind arch-rivals Celtic at the head of the Premiership, were throwing everything bar the kitchen sink at their hosts.

Balls were being blazed high and wide of the target. Chances were being passed up left, right and centre. It looked like Derek McInnes’ men were destined to rack up a third straight away draw in the league and take the club’s record to three years without a win at Fir Park when, in the 85th minute, substitute Findlay Curtis saw an effort parried by Alex Paulsen, Dujon Sterling blasted the rebound towards goal and Motherwell’s No 1 somehow flung an arm in the air and diverted it onto the crossbar.

It looked like the last throw of the dice. Until Ryan Naderi, who had suffered a miserable evening up to that point, made the difference.

A speculative shot from Badredine Bouanani from the edge of the area whacked off the outstretched boot of Martin Moormann and fell into the Czech internationalist’s path on the right.

His jabbed effort towards goal was nothing to write home about, but it carried just enough juice on it to whack off the hapless Moormann again, change direction and fly into the net.

Messy? Yes. Did Naderi care, though? Not a bit. He ran straight into the Rangers crowd behind the goal and lost himself in the relief and jubilation of a victory rescued from the fire.

That’s all that matters right now. Rangers won to keep up the pressure at the head of the table.

Naderi celebrates his late winner that snatched all three points for Rangers

McInnes applauds the travelling supporters after his side kept pace with Celtic at the top

However, there is a recurring problem with this squad. This game should have been out of sight, but missing chances and lacking that killer instinct manager McInnes demands remains a serious problem.

Just look at the stats. Rangers had 29 shots on goal in this affair and 11 on target. It should have been a procession, really. In the end, they only got through by the skin of their teeth.

There are times when these players look like they couldn’t hit a cow on the backside with a banjo and that is going to trip them up big-time in this title race unless they sort it out tout-suite.

They started like a runaway train in this game and got off to the perfect start with Manny Fernandez heading home from a corner within the first 10 minutes.

The problems started when Naderi, just nowhere as convincing in the role of main striker as he is when played with the likes of Kevin Kelsy, benched last night before a late cameo, up beside him, started missing sitters.

Jake Girdwood-Reich then levelled for Motherwell with pretty much their first forage upfield and it all got way more uncomfortable than it should have been. It is something McInnes is going to have to sort out.

The match started exactly the way McInnes would have wanted following the return from the international break with Rangers in the ascendancy from the first whistle and a goal to the good after eight minutes.

It was also as straightforward and as simple a goal as you could wish to see. One from a set-piece which Motherwell really ought to look back upon with some serious self-reflection. It was just too easy.

Djeidi Gassama had won a corner on the left thanks to a cross being deflected wide by Tom Sparrow. Kim Minsu fired in the flag-kick and Fernandez rose unchallenged to nod the ball home from close range. Like taking candy off a baby.

Fernandez gets his head to Minsu's corner to put Rangers in front early on at Fir Park

Fernandez milked the celebrations in front of the home fans after netting his first goal of the season, but Minsu’s reaction was tinged with the same senses of jubilation and relief.

The South Korean had been getting himself in a twist over failing to deliver an assist so far in his Rangers career. Now he’s off the mark on that front, it’s time for him to satisfy the demands from McInnes for a goal as well.

Shortly after the opener, Naderi, leading the line in front of Minsu, with Kelsy having been left on the bench, should have made it two.

An initial chance fell to the Czech internationalist after a Gassama shot had broken to him in the area. Moormann, however, put in a fine tackle to deflect the ball wide for a corner-kick.

Minsu took charge of that situation and fed it to Gassama, whose shot from a central position was parried by Paulsen.

It fell perfectly for Naderi and he should have buried a close-range header that ended up being cleared by Moormann again.

Fail to take your chances when on top and the prospect of getting yourself into bother is always there — and that’s what happened to Rangers on 21 minutes.

Motherwell had barely been up the park. Barely been in the game. However, they won a corner on the right thanks to some decent forward play from Regan Charles-Cook, on for the injured Ibrahim Said, and made the very most of the set-piece.

Emmanuel Longelo played a short corner to Sparrow who fired a low ball into the area at pace.

Girdwood-Reich timed his diagonal run nicely to move into space in front of a static Olwethu Makhanya and his first-time effort with the right foot beat visiting goalkeeper Ivor Pandur to his right to settle in the bottom corner.

Girdwood-Reich turns home Sparrow's cross to equalise for the home side

Nico Raskin had a shot touched over by Paulsen just before the half-hour and, moments later, it took a good saving tackle from Fernandez at the other end to deny Seb Palmer-Houlden a shot at goal after he had surged into the area.

With Motherwell getting their tails up before the interval, a ragged-looking Rangers really needed something to get a grip back on the game. It came just before the break with a one-on-one chance squandered by Naderi.

He had done well to get himself into a position where he could see the whites of Paulsen’s eyes, but the home keeper came out on top in the end by getting down low and touching the striker’s angled shot wide for a corner.

After Dan Neil had sent a low sidefooted effort just wide from the edge of the area and Palmer-Houlden had forced a save from Pandur with an unconvincing effort, Rangers passed up a super opportunity a little before the hour mark.

Naderi did well to set up Minsu in an unmarked position on the left side of the area. That elusive first goal in Rangers colours — or, rather, the foul red-and-black mish-mash that is their ‘third kit’ — beckoned.

Unfortunately, Minsu’s effort was awful. A straight-up sclaff that indicated a player just trying too hard or actually beginning to let a lack of confidence or a touch of anxiety interfere with his technique.

Whatever the reality, his poorly hit shot was saved at the near post by Paulsen.

Rangers did come close when a Tuur Rommens cross was deflected by Sparrow onto his own near post and Gassama then blazed a terrible effort over from a promising position.

When Paulsen made that double save, it looked like Motherwell had done enough to get a valuable point until Naderi got the visitors over the line by hook or by crook near the death.

It shouldn’t take this much effort and pain for Rangers to win a game of football, though. They need to show they can be cold-eyed killers if they want to win this title.

#1301. Moyes Reveals Everton Team News For Brentford

David Moyes is hopeful he will have a fully-fit squad to choose from as Everton look to extend their impressive form away to Brentford on Monday night (8pm GMT).

After the recent international break, the Blues resume their Premier League campaign in west London aiming to cement their place in the top six of the table.

Ahead of his pre-match press conference at Finch Farm on Friday, Moyes was presented with a signed frame by his former Blues midfielder Leon Osman and current captain James Tarkowski to mark his record-breaking 593rd match in charge of Everton against Brentford on Monday.

And the Toffees boss was confident he will have all options available for his starting XI in the capital.

'Hopefully everybody will be fit and available on Monday night for the Brentford game," said Moyes. "We've not had anyone return from international duty with any problems. We've got another few days to go before game day so hopefully we won't pick up any."

Despite having a small squad to work with this season, Moyes also spoke about his desire to be flexible with his team selection when possible.

He added: "I want us to be flexible where we can alter things if we have to.

"I think the form of Harrison [Armstrong] and Jimmy [Garner] and Kiernan [Dewsbury-Hall] has made it easy to select [the midfield]. It's not always just the form.

"We want to choose the right games and not overplay them. But it is quite difficult when you don't have quite so many players."

Brentford will be without main striker Igor Thiago for the visit of the Toffees, the Brazil international serving the first game of a three-match suspension following his red card for violent conduct in the 2-0 loss to Brighton & Hove Albion before the recent international break. In his absence, veteran Callum Wilson is in line to lead the Bees' attack.

Meanwhile, centre-back Nathan Collins is a doubt after sustaining a knee injury during the Republic of Ireland’s 1-0 defeat by Austria last Saturday. The 25-year-old returned to Brentford for further assessment and missed the Republic of Ireland’s 3-0 victory over Kosovo on Tuesday.

Full-back Aaron Hickey is another concern after picking up a hamstring problem while playing for Scotland against Switzerland.

Assistants: Nick Hopton and Adrian Holmes

#1300. Rangers boss Derek McInnes salutes never-say-die attitude of his side and was always confident of the winning goal arriving

Published: 18:17 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 18:22 EST, 21 November 2026

Rangers manager Derek McInnes praised his side for having the mentality to grind out last-gasp winners and hailed their late victory over Motherwell as a ‘top-class performance’.

McInnes admits he would have liked a more comfortable evening from a match which saw his side fire 29 shots with 11 on target, but he was happy with the level of chance creation and delighted to see Ryan Naderi serve up yet another crucial goal with a deflected effort that made the difference two minutes from time.

Rangers had opened brightly with a Manny Fernandez goal on eight minutes, but looked like sliding to a third straight league draw away from home after Jake Girdwood-Reich had levelled for the home side in the first half.

‘I thought it was a very good, strong performance. I’ve just been told that every one of my outfield players had a shot,’ said McInnes, whose men are four points behind Celtic with a game in hand against Aberdeen at Ibrox on Tuesday.

‘I’ve never known a team who practice so much shooting, and crossing and finishing during the week. It was the only thing missing for us, I thought it was a top class performance.

‘Away from home in the Premiership, you’re never going to dominate a whole game. There were little spells Motherwell had on transitions, but our press was strong and we were aggressive. I’m just disappointed it took so long to get the winning goal.

Derek McInnes revels in the victory at Motherwell at full-time

Ryan naderi scored the dramatic late winner for Rangers as they closed the gap on Celtic

‘Equally, on the sidelines, I felt a goal was coming. It’s OK me feeling that, but I think the players feel it too and it’s important they do. It would have been such a body blow if we hadn’t found a winning goal, given the stats and the performance.

‘It’s a tough away game and it’s the first time we’ve won here in three years, so that illustrates that.

‘When we pick the bones out of it, there will be a lot of what we ask for in that game.

‘It’s good that we’ve got that in us, a last minute goal, because we know how important they are in a campaign. I’ve never found mental strength an issue for my side.

‘On this fantastic run, we’ve been very strong. We were by far the better team. We dominated the chances and a lot of what I was hoping for was there.

‘It was just that execution. We’ve had this story before, but, as long as we keep winning, I’m all right with that.

‘I’m getting asked about not putting teams to bed. That’s another away game with two goals. It’s four in a row now. In our last two home games, we’ve scored four and three, so scoring goals isn’t really causing a problem, even if people are looking for a negative.

‘I think that performance was an improvement from where we’ve been in recent weeks.’

McInnes also reserved special praise for matchwinner Naderi.

‘Ryan’s game is really strong at the minute. He looks like a very confident boy and so he should be,’ said the manager. ‘Wrongly now, when you think of Ryan or people ask me, it’s about him knocking his pan in.

‘His pressing is unbelievable and he’s a big horse up there. He runs and works and puts people under pressure, but he gets goals and has an influence. In that system tonight, his was the most important position for us, in terms of running channels and getting hold of the ball.

Manny Fernandez opened the scoring for the Ibrox men in the 2-1 victory

‘He led the line brilliantly. It was a proper No 9 performance.

Naderi admits he is delighted to be scoring messy goals that are making a real impact on his side’s challenge for the title.

‘I like those games. Of course we would like to win 3-0, but, when you win in the last minute, that's something special,’ said the Czech internationalist.

‘I can't score nice goals, only ugly ones.’

Motherwell head coach Alfred Johansson said: ‘It is obviously tough to concede that goal at the very end. We had a feeling we could finish the game with a draw.

‘I think Rangers were better than us. They had a good start to the game and it was tough for us conceding a goal from a set-piece when we are not aggressive enough.

‘At the end, we lost the energy. Rangers were turning up the heat in the last 15, 20 minutes. We were fighting and surviving and then they scored.

‘Alex Paulsen played fantastic in goal. He has been making a lot of saves for us this season and, at the end, it is tough for him to concede a goal like that.’

#1299. Surprise Presentation For Moyes Ahead Of Record-Breaking Fixture

David Moyes was presented with a commemorative frame ahead of Monday night’s Premier League away fixture against Brentford – a record-breaking match for the Everton manager.

The trip to the Gtech Community Stadium will mark Moyes’ 593rd game as Everton manager, taking him ahead of the legendary Harry Catterick in the all-time rankings.

Everton captain James Tarkowski and former Blues midfielder Leon Osman were on hand to present the signed frame – and Moyes said it’s a “privilege and honour” to have reached the historic milestone.

"I'm really thrilled about. I've become the manager who has managed more Everton games than anyone before. That's a privilege and an honour to be put in that position.

"I have to thank the people who brought me to the Club in the first place. When you take a chance on a young manager, you never know it'll be work, but they had great faith and believed in me.

"I'm so thankful for the people around Everton because they've been so good for me."

Handing over the frame, Osman said: “It’s a record I don’t think will ever be beaten – and I don’t say that lightly. This is some achievement for a huge football club.

“I’m sure James is like me in saying it’s been an honour to play for you. It’s been an honour, a privilege. It’s been hard! But you’ve made us all better and we wish you many more successes for the upcoming seasons.”

#1298. Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.
